Impossible Trinomial

GeometryParadoxes
Game: This is a picture to explore, not a game to win: one fork looks like two flat prongs at the left and three round tubes at the right.
How to play: Move the sliders to slide a cover over the drawing and see what the lines look like. Press Reset to see the whole fork again.

Left: two flat prongs. Right: three round ends. Both readings come from the same lines.

1
1
Look for the math

The cut-the-knot page says that the fork, on the left, appears to extend two rectangular prongs that, on the right, metamorphose into three cylinders. Nothing changes in the drawing to make that happen: only the way your eye joins the lines changes.

One drawing, two readings

Count what is really there. The applet draws 6 long horizontal lines and 3 oval ends, one on every other line. At the left, a short slant closes the lowest pair of lines into one prong, and three slants close the next lines into a second, diamond-shaped prong. So the page's claim holds in the drawing: two prong ends at the left, three round ends at the right. This is an impossible object — a flat optical illusion, not a solid thing you could build.

How the lines are placed

The old applet measures its canvas as w across and h down, then sets t = h / 7, X = t / 2, Y = t / √3 and Z = 7w / 15, rounding the divisions to whole numbers. The three ovals sit 2Y apart on lines 1, 3 and 5. The logic test checks all 9,801 canvas sizes in the applet's range against a second transcription of those instructions, and they agree.

The cover changes the reading, not the picture

The two sliders paint a background-coloured band of width W% starting D% of the remaining width from the left edge. Sliding it can hide the middle of the fork, or all but a sliver. Yet the six lines and three ovals underneath never move: that is the invariant the test checks for all 60 × 110 slider settings. Your brain wants to see perspective and a real three-dimensional object; the drawing quietly refuses to be one.

Try cover width 60 and position 30, then slide the position to 110. The fork looks completely different, but every line is still exactly where it was.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
